## What controls the temperature of an object?

-   Incoming energy

-   Outgoing energy

-   The heat capacity of the object (how much energy is needed to heat a degree)

-   Incoming \> Outgoing = warming

-   Incoming \< Outgoing = cooling

## What controls Earth's temperature?

-   Incoming: energy received by the sun
-   Outgoing: reflection of sun's energy (albedo)
-   Outgoing: Energy released by Earth
-   Net: The amount of energy retained by the earth's atmosphere.

## Amount of energy received from the sun

::::: columns
::: {.column width="40%"}
-   Sunspots -- reflect the magnetic activity of the sun and the sun's brightness.
-   Approximately an 11-year cycle
-   Not getting brighter over last 30 years
:::

::: {.column width="60%"}
![](img/solar-cycles2.png){fig-alt="graph of 11-year solar cycles"}
:::
:::::

## Amount of energy received by the sun

::::: columns
::: {.column width="70%"}
-   The path of the earth around the sun and the earth's angle vary at different time scales.
-   Has been an important influence for glacial periods (every 100,000 years) over the past 500,000 years.
-   Milankovitch Cycles
:::

::: {.column width="30%"}
![](img/solar-cycles1.png){fig-alt="image different components of Milankovitch Cycles"}
:::
:::::

## Amount of energy reflected to space {.smaller}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="70%"}
-   Albedo (reflectivity)
-   Lighter things reflect more light energy
-   Darker things absorb more light energy (heat)
-   Creates positive feedback
-   Aerosols lead to increased reflection of solar radiation (Volcanic activity -\> cooling).
:::

::: {.column width="30%"}
![](img/albedo.png){fig-alt="diagram of earth's albedo"}
:::
:::::

## Amount of energy retained by the atmosphere

-   Solar energy absorbed by land/oceans is converted into heat
-   Objects with heat release energy in proportion to their heat
-   Sun = HOT, Earth = Not Hot, so energy release by energy is different than heat released by sun


## Amount of energy retained by the atmosphere

::::: columns
::: {.column width="40%"}
-   The greenhouse effect: Some of energy in the form released by earth surface is absorbed by the atmosphere
-   Gases in the atmosphere trap heat (H20, CO2, CH4, NOxs, CFCs)
-   Trapped heat is remitted by the atmosphere towards the surface
-   Now the surface is heated by sun and the energy from the gases in the atmosphere
-   Greenhouse effect is good because earth would be too cold without it! 
-   But changing due to changing gases in the atmosphere
:::

::: {.column width="60%"}
![](img/ghg.png){fig-alt="diagram of greenhouse gas influence on earth's energy"}
:::
:::::

## Why does climate change matter?

- Climate has always changed and will always change
- Historically major climate change has been associated with massive changes in life on earth
  - Alaska was subtropical when early humans cross the land-bridge
  - The entire Earth has been cover with ice in the past
  - If change is faster than life can adapt or evolve, then challenging for current life
  
  
## Why does climate change matter?

- Do we want to want live in the warmer world?
  - What does a warmer world look like? (Impacts)
  - Winners and losers
- If humans are causing it, then we can stop causing it.
  - Should we? At what costs?
  - Winners and losers

## Data: What is "global temperature"?

Global surface temperature is calculated by averaging the temperatures over sea and land. Communicated as an anomaly.

![](img/global-temp-map.png){fig-alt="global map of surface temperature"}

## Data: What is "global temperature"?

-   Many groups across the world have generated datasets of global temperature
-   One example: Hansen et al. 2010 from Goddard Institute for Space Studies, NASA http://pubs.giss.nasa.gov/docs/2010/2010_Hansen_etal_1.pdf
-   Different datasets from weather stations all over the world were compiled.
-   Used a model to interpolate (smooth) data for land
-   Use bucket (ships) and satellite measurements calibrated with ship measurements for the ocean

## What would cause global temperature to change?

-  Sun increasing output (Not likely)
-  Earth relatively closer to the sun (not the current cycle)
-  Color of the earth getting darker (actually getting brighter due to agriculture)
-  More greenhouse gasses in the atmosphere (👈)
   - Primarily from fossil fuel composition

## How do we measure atmospheric CO2?

::::: columns
::: {.column width="60%"}
-   Dr. Dave Keeling started measuring the CO2 concentration in air in 1958
-   Collected air in vacuum-cleared glass flasks and measured CO2 content
-   Still measured with the method today (as well as sensors)
:::

::: {.column width="40%"}
![](img/mauna-lao.png){fig-alt="map of Mauna Loa"}
:::
:::::

## How do current changes compare to past climate?

-   The earth is 4.54 billion years old
-   The last ice age was 110,000 to 12,000 years ago, with peak glaciation 22,000 years ago
-   The world looked different!
    -   Northern USA and Canada covered by ice
    -   Southern US covered by taiga (coniferous forest) and grassland
    -   Southern Europe was tundra
